blocks.title: Why pgvector for RAG matters here

spans.text: Problem statement: A SaaS app stores embeddings in Postgres so docs search can share existing auth and backups. The learner's job is not to memorize pgvector for RAG; it is to decide what to build or change, what evidence the system may use, and how to tell whether the change improved query latency and recall on real support questions.

Running case: pgvector schema, indexing, and retrieval checklist. We will keep this same case through the lesson so each idea has a job: frame the problem, explain the mechanism, choose a design, test the implementation, and decide what to do next.

Before reading on, predict: if embedding dimensions or index settings mismatch the model in production, where would you look first - the input, the state or data, the model boundary, the validation check, or the release process?
The lesson assumes you can learn the vocabulary, then spends its effort on integration choices, failure signals, and checks that make the idea usable in a real system.

items.text: Product framing: pgvector for RAG matters when it changes a user-visible decision, release gate, or operational workflow.
Engineering framing: pgvector for RAG matters when it changes data, state, prompts, model behavior, tools, schemas, traces, or runtime constraints.
Validation framing: the lesson is not complete until the team can measure query latency and recall on real support questions on examples that resemble the real workload.

blocks.title: Fully worked example: pgvector schema, indexing, and retrieval checklist

spans.text: Scenario: A SaaS app stores embeddings in Postgres so docs search can share existing auth and backups. The team wants to improve query latency and recall on real support questions, but it has already seen this failure: embedding dimensions or index settings mismatch the model in production.
Here is the worked artifact at design-review depth: concrete enough to inspect, small enough to build as a thin slice.
Complete worked artifact

items.text: Question: "Can I get a refund after 35 days if I lost my invoice?" The answer must cite the exact policy chunk, not a plausible refund rule remembered by the model.

Artifact: pgvector schema, indexing, and retrieval checklist. It specifies loaders, chunk metadata, retriever settings, prompt contract, citation format, and a faithfulness check for query latency and recall on real support questions.
Worked output: retrieve policy-refunds-v3 section 4, quote "30 days" and "invoice id required", answer that the request probably fails the policy, and link the source chunk used.

spans.text: Complete AI-assistant prompt for this artifact

Role: RAG reviewer. Context: A SaaS app stores embeddings in Postgres so docs search can share existing auth and backups. Task: inspect pgvector schema, indexing, and retrieval checklist. Require a user question, retrieved chunks with source ids, final answer, and a claim-by-claim support check. Constraints: do not allow claims that are absent from retrieved chunks; flag stale or missing metadata. Output: {question, retrieved_sources, answer, unsupported_claims, release_decision}.
Why this is richer than a definition
The example ties pgvector for RAG to a specific input, output, decision, failure mode, and metric. That is the move you should repeat when applying the lesson to your own system.

blocks.title: Case study: what changed after the first review

spans.text: The first prototype works on the demo path. Then a reviewer runs the uncomfortable case: embedding dimensions or index settings mismatch the model in production. The output still looks confident, which is exactly why the lesson needs a richer artifact.

The team does not restart from scratch. It adds one missing control to pgvector schema, indexing, and retrieval checklist: a stricter input contract, better source metadata, a validation assertion, a human-review edge, a rollback trigger, or an audit log depending on where the failure appeared.

items.text: Decision made: keep the thin slice, but block release until the failure is observable and repeatable.
Evidence added: the artifact now shows the input, intermediate evidence, final output, and pass/fail reason.
Metric promoted: query latency and recall on real support questions becomes part of the release gate instead of a dashboard someone checks later.

blocks.title: How this breaks in practice

spans.text: The failure mode to keep in view is concrete: embedding dimensions or index settings mismatch the model in production. Use it as a diagnostic lens while reading every design choice.

items.text: Retrieved chunks mention the right keyword but not the answer-bearing paragraph.
The answer is relevant but unfaithful: it adds a policy or fact not present in the retrieved evidence.
Metadata is missing, so citations cannot be checked or reranked later.
The broad warning sign: query latency and recall on real support questions gets worse even though the final answer or artifact still looks polished.

spans.text: Debugging rule: inspect the earliest place where bad evidence can enter and the latest place where validation should have stopped it.
